There isn't one best combo for every RV. It depends on whether you run the roof AC on battery, and on how much solar you can fit. These are the setups I'd consider, based on the guides I read. I didn't find a tested, specific panel bundle, so the panel advice is sizing guidance and not a named product.

**1. Full-time boondocking: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3**
- It has 4,096Wh (expandable past 12kWh), 4,000W continuous and 8,000W surge. It recharges 0–80% in about 50 minutes from a wall outlet.
- It's heavy enough to need two people to move. It's also the priciest option once you add expansion batteries.
- [Check it on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=ecoflow+delta+pro+3&tag=ggref-20) (source: [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))

**2. Running the roof AC on weekends: Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro**
- It has 3,024Wh, 3,000W continuous and 6,000W surge, which is enough to start a 13,500 BTU AC. It has simple physical buttons.
- The AC runs only about 1.7 hours per charge. There's no 30A RV outlet, so you need a dogbone adapter. It weighs about 64 lb.
- [Check it on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=jackery+explorer+3000+pro&tag=ggref-20)

**3. Best value with a built-in 30A RV port: BLUETTI AC200L**
- It has 2,048Wh and 2,400W (3,600W surge). Wall charging takes it to 80% in about 45 minutes. It takes solar directly.
- It has no 240V output, and the AC drains it fast.
- [Check it on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=bluetti+ac200l&tag=ggref-20)

**Other options**
- **Anker SOLIX F2600:** 2,560Wh, 2,400W, 30A port, 5-year warranty. It's just under 70 lb and its solar input is lower. [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=anker+solix+f2600&tag=ggref-20)
- **Goal Zero Yeti 1500X:** the lightest at about 44 lb, with 1,516Wh. It suits small trailers and solar-first setups. It needs a soft-start kit to run an AC. [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=goal+zero+yeti+1500x&tag=ggref-20)
- **ALLPOWERS R4000:** 3,456Wh, 3,600W at 120V, LiFePO4, 5-year warranty, with an RV outlet. It accepts up to 2,000W of solar over three inputs (650W each). It's listed at $1,499, or $1,319.12 with code EXTRA12, which the deal site says it tested on Oct 23 and which expires Nov 15. It weighs 45 kg (about 99 lb), so it's more of a permanent install. [Buy at ALLPOWERS](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-r4000-3456wh) (this is a commission link, and I haven't checked the price myself)

**Choosing solar panels**
- **Check the station's solar input limit.** A guide I read ([GetWattLogic](https://getwattlogic.com/articles/bluetti-vs-jackery-vs-ecoflow-van-life)) says a big roof array can be capped by a lower input rating.
- **Use a 300–400W folding array for mid-size stations.** One guide says that refills one in a decent summer day. Expect less in spring and fall. A larger array only pays off if the station can accept it.
- **Buy panels from the same brand as the station** for easy connectors and compatibility. Confirm the connector type and voltage range on the station's spec page.

**How to pick**
- **Roof AC on battery:** you need 2,000W continuous and 3,500W surge or better. A 13,500 BTU unit draws about 1,500W running and spikes above 3,000W at startup.
- **Fridge, lights, laptop and Starlink only:** a 1–2kWh unit with a 300W panel is probably enough.
- **Weight:** anything over 60 lb should stay in the RV.

The EmergencyEnergy guide is written for Ontario, Canada. The specs apply, but its electrical-code advice doesn't. Prices change, so check the retailer page before you buy.

If you tell me your RV's size, whether you have a roof AC, and how many nights off-grid you want, I can narrow this to one station and a panel size.

 Compare five RV power stations for 2026 on running watts, surge output, runtime and noise, plus Ontario safety rules for campsite and boondocking power.

 [Frequently Asked Questions](#frequently-asked-questions)
 [What Should You Remember?](#what-should-you-remember)
 RV season in Ontario runs from the May long weekend to Thanksgiving, and the electrical pedestals at most provincial parks top out at 30 amps. That is enough for lights, a fridge and a laptop charger. Add a roof air conditioner or an induction cooktop and the pedestal breaker trips. A portable power station fills that gap, and unlike a gas generator it can run inside the coach or under the awning with no exhaust at all. If you already own a small unit for tailgates, our [portable power station guide](/articles/best-portable-power-station-2026/) explains where those compact models stop being useful. This comparison covers five units that hold up under real trailer loads.
 The picks below were sorted on four measured numbers: continuous AC output, surge output, usable capacity and charge time. Real campsite loads matter far more than the number on the box. A 13,500 BTU roof air conditioner draws about 1,500W running and spikes past 3,000W on compressor startup, so a station rated at 1,000W will not get it off the line no matter what the marketing claims. Runtime figures here are calculated at 85 percent inverter efficiency, which is where most lithium units land under a steady 500W load. There is a second use case worth naming. [Outage statistics](/articles/emergency-power-statistics-2026/) show that the same battery you carry in the trailer can keep a furnace fan and fridge alive at home during a winter storm.
 Safety rules do not soften because the power source is smaller. RV shore inlets, transfer switches and any permanent wiring in a trailer fall under Ontario electrical rules, and the [Electrical Safety Authority](https://esasafe.com/) requires a licensed electrician for anything beyond plugging into an existing outlet. Carbon monoxide is the other hard line. Battery stations produce none, which is why one can sit on the dinette table, but a gas generator stays outside and away from windows and vents. The [CSA Group](https://www.csagroup.org/) publishes the standards behind both the appliances and the CO alarms you should have on board, and our [generator safety guide](/articles/generator-safety-tips/) covers placement distances in detail.
 Choosing comes down to three questions. How many watts does your largest single load need at startup? How many hours do you need it to run? How much weight can you lift into a storage bay? A 2,000Wh station weighs between 40 and 55 pounds, which one person can handle. Anything above 3,000Wh usually means two people or a dedicated cart. Solar input matters as well, since most Ontario parks enforce quiet hours and a 300W to 400W folding array will refill a mid-size unit in a full day of decent sun. Buy for the load you actually run, not the one you imagine running.

 Bluetti vs Jackery vs EcoFlow for Van Life (2026)

 Bluetti vs Jackery vs EcoFlow for Van Life (2026)
 If you're shopping for a portable power station for a van, RV, or off-grid rig, you've almost certainly landed on these three names. All three now build their main lineups around LiFePO4 (LFP) battery chemistry — the same durable, thermally stable chemistry recommended throughout this site — so the decision usually comes down to how each brand is positioned rather than a clear "better" or "worse" pick.
 Here's how they generally differ, and which one fits which kind of build.
 The short version
 Bluetti — best for expandability and solar input. If you're planning to grow your system over time or want to pair with a large panel array, Bluetti's higher solar input ceilings and modular accessory ecosystem make it the easiest to build around long-term.
 Jackery — best for straightforward portability and ecosystem polish. If you want something that works well out of the box with minimal setup and solid outdoor-oriented accessories, Jackery leans hardest into that use case.
 EcoFlow — best for charging speed and raw output. If fast recharge (wall or generator) matters to your routine — say, you're moving between camp spots often and want a quick top-up — EcoFlow's charging speed is its standout feature across most of its lineup.
 What actually matters for van life specifically
 Solar input ceiling. Not every power station accepts the same maximum solar wattage. If you're running a rooftop array on a van or RV — rather than a small folding panel — check the unit's rated solar input before assuming your panels will actually deliver their full output. This is one of the more common mismatch points in van builds: a well-sized panel array bottlenecked by a power station's lower solar input ceiling.
 Weight and footprint. Vans and RVs have hard limits on payload and storage space in a way that cabins and homes don't. Portability-focused designs generally trade some capacity-per-dollar for a lighter, more compact form factor — worth weighing directly against your specific rig's available space.
 Expandability. Some models in each brand's lineup support add-on battery modules to grow capacity after your initial purchase, rather than requiring a full unit swap. If you expect your power needs to grow — adding a fridge, later going full-time — this is worth checking before you commit to a fixed-capacity unit.
 Charging speed. How you actually recharge matters more than the spec sheet suggests. If you're relying primarily on solar, recharge speed from a wall outlet or generator matters less. If you're moving frequently and topping up from campground power or a generator between stops, faster recharge times translate directly into less downtime.
 Chemistry: why LiFePO4 matters
 Across all three brands, the main current-generation lineups have shifted to LiFePO4 chemistry, which offers a meaningfully longer cycle life (commonly rated in the thousands of charge cycles to 80% capacity) than older lithium-ion designs, along with better thermal stability. Some older or lower-tier models — across any of these brands — may still use older chemistry, so it's worth confirming the battery chemistry of the specific model you're considering rather than assuming based on brand alone.
 How to actually decide
 The honest answer is that all three brands are credible, and the "best" one depends on your specific loadout and habits more than brand loyalty. That's exactly what the calculator on this site solves — instead of matching your build to a brand's marketing positioning, it sizes your battery capacity from your actual devices and usage, so you know what capacity, solar input, and inverter rating you actually need before you start comparing specific models.
